title: Embedding Vocabulary in Foundational Skills Work
author: Science of Reading Classroom
summary: This post follows up on an SRI International report finding that early-literacy foundational skills lessons often fail to connect word recognition with language comprehension. Here the focus is the report's second finding: in over half of observed lessons, vocabulary and word meaning were addressed once or not at all. The authors argue this is a missed opportunity, especially for multilingual learners, because short conversations about meaning can be woven into skills work at little cost. They illustrate with a kindergarten teacher, Anjanette McNeely, whose three-minute word blending drill references word meaning at least eight times without losing its purpose. McNeely explains how she chooses words on the fly and why the curse of expertise hides which words children do not know. The post ends with a practical recommendation that teams scan upcoming lessons during PLC or planning time and decide in advance which words deserve elaboration.
points: The SRI finding that vocabulary was addressed once or not at all in over half of foundational skills lessons shows that decoding instruction and meaning-making are still being separated in practice.

The model drill demonstrates that vocabulary can be embedded without derailing the routine, as long as the teacher waits until students are comfortable with the blending routine before adding meaning.
Effective embedded vocabulary work is active, with choral responses, student sentences and movement, rather than a teacher-delivered definition.
The curse of expertise explains why teachers overlook unknown words in short, simple-looking decodable text, since adults hear those words as automatic.
Because curricula rarely flag words worth elaborating, the authors suggest teams use PLC time to pre-select multi-meaning or unfamiliar words in upcoming lessons.
quotes: But the report shared another important finding: “many lessons missed opportunities to embed vocabulary development within foundational skills instruction.” In fact, in over half of the lessons, vocabulary and word meaning were addressed once or not at all.

Quick conversations about multiple meanings, generating synonyms or antonyms, connecting words to movements, and asking students to share examples are all efficient ways to grow and solidify comprehension, while also doing meaningful foundational skills work at the same time.
The vocabulary work never derails or distracts from the purpose of drill: blending practice. You’ll also notice that she doesn’t discuss every single word.

It is easy to assume that because these are short words, students will know what they mean. I think that is the curse of expertise because as adults, we have been exposed to these words so many times that their meanings feel automatic.

In an ideal world, curriculum developers would make this integration easier for teachers by highlighting words worth elaborating on in the teacher’s manual and perhaps offerings some student-friendly examples or definitions.
Scan the upcoming lessons, identify which words are worth elaborating on (words with multiple meanings and uses, words students might not know), and decide how you might address them in the lesson.
